$comment: Rules for producing a sanitized file. §5.2 makes originals immutable and §9.3 forbids in-place overwrite, so every remediation writes somewhere new and says where. Data, not prose: tools/output-naming.mjs is checked against this table by the validator, in both directions.

naming.$comment: report.pdf -> 'report (sanitized).pdf' -> 'report (sanitized) 2.pdf'. The marker goes before the final extension so the file stays openable by the same application, which is the point of §11.1's collision-safe filenames.
naming.extensionRuleLimit: A name with two meaningful extensions, archive.tar.gz, becomes 'archive.tar (sanitized).gz'. The MVP media types in §8.1 all carry one extension, so this is stated and vectored rather than solved here.

writeProtocol.$comment: A name is claimed by creating it exclusively, not by asking whether it exists. Asking leaves a window in which another process answers the same question the same way, which is exactly the concurrent case §20.2 requires.
writeProtocol.tempLocationReason: A rename is atomic only within one filesystem. A temp file elsewhere degrades silently into a copy, and a partially copied file that carries the destination's name is the one thing §12.1 says must never appear.

destination_exists.rationale: an explicit output path already names a file. §9.3 forbids overwriting; an explicit path is a statement about where to write, not permission to replace what is there.

no_free_name.rationale: the sequence was exhausted without claiming a name. Continuing without a claim would mean writing to a name nothing reserved.

temp_outside_destination_directory.rationale: the temporary file is not beside its destination, so the rename would cross filesystems and stop being atomic. A copy that fails halfway leaves a file wearing the destination's name.

temp_name_taken.rationale: the temporary name belongs to another run. Writing to it anyway would destroy a half-written file - the collision the destination is careful about, one name over.
